clue.text: Put brakes on engineers' transport

parts.note: RE stands for the Royal Engineers, a British army corps, and the possessive adds S
a train is a means of transport

explanation.surface: Someone halts the vehicle the army engineers use.
explanation.walkthrough: The possessive S of 'engineers'' is kept here as a letter: RE (Royal Engineers) plus S.
explanation.definitionFit: To curb or check something is to slow it, as a brake does a vehicle.

clue.text: Rules, for example, used in verse

indicators.note: one piece is said to be employed inside another, so it goes within it

parts.note: rimes is an old spelling of rhymes, i.e. verse

explanation.surface: Grammar or metre rules being illustrated within a poem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rules' looks like a verb but is a plural noun; 'used in' is the container signal, and rimes is an archaic spelling of rhymes.
explanation.definitionFit: Regimes are systems of government, the ones who rule a country.

clue.text: Cat, alas, in trouble — like Macavity?

indicators.note: letters in trouble are thrown into disorder, so these words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A lament for a cat in difficulties, Macavity being T. S. Eliot's criminal cat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' looks like part of the phrase 'in trouble' but is fodder; 'trouble' alone signals the anagram of CATALASIN. Macavity, in T. S. Eliot's poems, is described as a fiend in feline shape.
explanation.definitionFit: Devilish, the adjective of the Devil, suits Eliot's fiendish feline criminal.

clue.text: Traveller allowed key is satisfied

parts.note: a rep is a travelling sales representative

explanation.surface: A salesman permitted to proceed is content.
explanation.walkthrough: A rep is short for a sales representative, who travels between customers.
explanation.definitionFit: Being full after a meal is to be fed up to contentment.

clue.text: Only big letters written so low

indicators.note: the letters are written out again in a new order, signalling a rearrangement

explanation.surface: Only large capitals are written at such a small size.
explanation.walkthrough: 'letters written' signals an anagram of ONLY BIG.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting basely or dishonourably is behaving in a mean, base manner.

clue.text: Delay caused loss of interest

explanation.surface: Something was postponed and the audience got bored.
explanation.definitionFit: Postponing an event, and repelling someone so their enthusiasm wanes, are both senses of the phrasal verb.

clue.text: Next churchman holds symbol of St Luke

indicators.note: one piece holds another, so the second sits inside the first

parts.note: a primate is an archbishop or chief bishop
the evangelist Luke is traditionally symbolised by an ox

explanation.surface: A senior cleric carries the emblem of the Gospel writer Luke.
explanation.definitionFit: Nearest or immediately adjoining, as in a proximate cause, is the closest one in sequence.

clue.text: Formidable lady opponent likely to scratch?

explanation.surface: A fierce woman is a rival who fights with her nails.
explanation.definitionFit: A fierce, strong-willed woman is called this, and a big female cat literally uses claws.

clue.text: Such tact may be needed when king or queen's missing

definitions.text: Such tact may be needed when king or queen's missing

parts.words: Such tact may be needed when king or queen's missing
parts.note: reads as diplomacy at a royal absence, but at bridge a delicate play is made to win a trick when an opponent may hold the missing high card

explanation.surface: Diplomacy is called for when a monarch has gone absent.
explanation.definitionFit: Delicate skill in handling people is tact, and the same word names a bridge play.

clue.text: Rise and depart for drive

parts.note: to get up is to rise

explanation.surface: Get out of bed and leave in order to go for a drive.
explanation.definitionFit: Energy and enthusiasm, as in a person with plenty of drive.

clue.text: Working group to go North of the border

definitions.text: to go North of the border

explanation.surface: A team of workers heads up to Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'North of the border' means in Scotland, where gang is a dialect word for go.
explanation.definitionFit: A squad of labourers works together, and in Scots the verb means to walk or go.

clue.text: Suspicious activity in the zoo?

explanation.surface: Something shady is going on among the zoo animals.
explanation.definitionFit: Mischief or underhand dealings, and literally the doings of apes and their kin.

clue.text: Company so established, initially, in financial centre

parts.note: the City is London's financial district

indicators.note: initially means take only the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A firm set up this way first appears in the City.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initially' gives E from 'established', and 'in' puts it inside CITY, the City of London.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in someone's company is being in their society, the companionship of others.

clue.text: Bird changes colour

parts.note: turns means changes, as leaves turn
a tone is a shade of colour

explanation.surface: A bird alters its plumage colour.
explanation.definitionFit: A shore wader that flips pebbles hunting for food.

clue.text: Rodent which Amsterdam traps

indicators.note: the phrase traps letters inside it, signalling a run concealed across the words

explanation.surface: A small rodent caught in the Dutch capital.
explanation.definitionFit: A small furry pet of the mouse family is a rodent.

clue.text: Like some watches, requiring a couple of people

explanation.surface: Some timepieces need two people to operate them.
explanation.definitionFit: A clock face with hour and minute hands, and a task such as sawing that needs two workers.

clue.text: Part of mine used to show pictures

explanation.surface: Part of the colliery is used as an exhibition space.
explanation.definitionFit: A horizontal tunnel in a mine, and a room or building for displaying art.

clue.text: Saint has porridge in the morning

parts.note: brose is a Scottish oatmeal dish like porridge

explanation.surface: A holy man eats oatmeal at breakfast.
explanation.walkthrough: Brose is a Scottish dish of oatmeal mixed with boiling water.
explanation.definitionFit: St Ambrose was a fourth-century bishop of Milan.

clue.text: Left, heading East for French port

indicators.note: one piece heads the other, so it comes first

explanation.surface: Someone departs, making eastward for a harbour in France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heading' puts L in front of ORIENT.
explanation.definitionFit: Lorient is a naval harbour town in Brittany.

clue.text: Outside broadcast can be so dull

indicators.note: broadcast means scattered widely, so the letters are scattered into a new order

explanation.surface: A TV programme filmed on location can be boring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outside broadcast' reads as a TV term, but 'broadcast' signals an anagram of OUTSIDE.
explanation.definitionFit: Boring and wearisome is the same as dull.

clue.text: High point of course? Excellent

explanation.surface: The best hole on the golf course is first-rate.
explanation.walkthrough: Top-hole is dated British slang for excellent.
explanation.definitionFit: The uppermost green of a golf course, and old-fashioned slang for first-rate.

clue.text: Reveal bodies, perhaps? That's about right

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the rearranged letters go round the other piece
perhaps hints the word bodies can be read in another order

explanation.surface: Is stripping off to bare bodies acceptable?
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' turns BODIES into DISOBE, and 'about' puts it round R.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking off one's clothes exposes the body beneath.

clue.text: Second auditor one employed to handle fleecing

parts.note: an auditor is literally a listener, one who hears

explanation.surface: A second accountant was hired to deal with a swindle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'auditor' and 'fleecing' suggest accounting fraud, but an auditor is a listener, and fleecing is cutting wool.
explanation.definitionFit: A sheep-clipper removes the wool coat from the flock.

clue.text: Transient visitors flock in a way

explanation.surface: Short-stay guests arrive in a crowd along a route.
explanation.definitionFit: People who stay only briefly, and migrating flocks literally travelling a route.

clue.text: Nothing can be blamed for global revolution

definitions.text: can be blamed for global revolution

explanation.surface: Nobody can be held responsible for the world's upheaval.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition plays on the saying that this makes the world go round; it is also the tennis score for nil.
explanation.definitionFit: A zero score in tennis, and the affection said to make the world go round.

clue.text: Dismissed from brotherhood for not working

explanation.surface: A monk expelled from his order is now unemployed.
explanation.definitionFit: Expelled from a religious fraternity, and broken or not functioning.

clue.text: Captain can cook fish

explanation.surface: A ship's master is able to prepare seafood.
explanation.walkthrough: Captain Kettle was a fictional sea captain in popular Victorian adventure stories; a fish kettle is a long pan for poaching fish.
explanation.definitionFit: A fictional sea skipper of that name, and a long metal pan for poaching fish.

clue.text: Advocate is back in team

explanation.surface: The lawyer is also a full-back in the side.
explanation.definitionFit: A champion of a cause, and a player in a defensive position in a team sport.
